problem.summary: 在移动设备等计算资源极其有限（10-150 MFLOPs）的平台上，部署高精度的卷积神经网络（CNN）面临巨大挑战。现有高效架构（如Xception、ResNeXt）中的1×1卷积（逐点卷积）计算成本高昂，在极小网络中限制了通道数量，从而损害了精度。

motivation.summary: 移动设备（如无人机、机器人、智能手机）对高效CNN的需求日益增长。现有工作多关注于对“基础”网络进行剪枝、压缩或低比特表示，而本文旨在探索一种专门为极低计算预算设计的高效基础架构。

core_idea.summary: 提出ShuffleNet架构，其核心创新在于引入两个新操作：1) 逐点分组卷积（Pointwise Group Convolution），以大幅降低1×1卷积的计算成本；2) 通道混洗（Channel Shuffle），以解决分组卷积堆叠导致的信息流阻塞问题，实现跨组信息交换。

method.summary: ShuffleNet的基本单元（ShuffleNet Unit）由逐点分组卷积、通道混洗和深度可分离卷积（Depthwise Convolution）构成。通过调整分组数g和缩放因子s，可以灵活控制网络复杂度和精度。网络整体架构包含多个阶段，每个阶段由多个ShuffleNet单元堆叠而成。

experiments.summary: 在ImageNet分类任务和MS COCO目标检测任务上进行了广泛实验。实验包括：1) 与MobileNet、VGG-like、ResNet、Xception-like、ResNeXt等结构的对比；2) 对分组数g和通道混洗操作的消融研究；3) 在ARM移动设备上的实际推理速度评估。

claims.claim: ShuffleNet在极低计算预算（如40 MFLOPs）下，相比MobileNet等现有架构，能实现显著更高的分类精度（如绝对降低7.8%的top-1错误率）。
通道混洗操作对于分组卷积堆叠的性能至关重要，能有效促进跨组信息流动。
ShuffleNet在实际移动设备上能实现显著的加速（如相比AlexNet实现约13倍的实际加速）。
ShuffleNet架构设计简单，易于与其他先进技术（如Squeeze-and-Excitation模块）结合。

limitations.limitation: 1) 深度可分离卷积在低功耗移动设备上的实际效率可能受限于较差的计算/内存访问比。2) 较大的分组数（如g=8）在当前实现中实际推理效率较低。3) 论文主要关注分类和检测任务，在其他任务上的泛化能力未充分验证。

nodes.title: 逐点分组卷积 (Pointwise Group Convolution)
nodes.label: 核心操作
nodes.summary: 将标准的1×1卷积替换为分组卷积，显著降低计算复杂度。
nodes.description: 对于输入特征图，将其通道分为g组，每组独立进行1×1卷积。这使得计算成本从O(c_in * c_out)降低到O((c_in * c_out) / g)。这是ShuffleNet实现高效计算的关键之一。

nodes.title: 通道混洗 (Channel Shuffle)
nodes.label: 核心操作
nodes.summary: 在分组卷积层之间对通道进行重新排列，以实现跨组信息流动。
nodes.description: 在两个连续的分组卷积层之间，对输出通道的顺序进行重新排列（混洗），使得下一层分组卷积的输入来自上一层的不同组。这解决了分组卷积堆叠导致的信息流阻塞问题。

nodes.title: ShuffleNet单元 (ShuffleNet Unit)
nodes.label: 基本构建块
nodes.summary: 由逐点分组卷积、通道混洗和深度可分离卷积组成的高效残差单元。
nodes.description: ShuffleNet单元是网络的基本构建块。它包含：1) 一个1×1逐点分组卷积用于降维；2) 一个3×3深度可分离卷积；3) 另一个1×1逐点分组卷积用于升维。在第一个1×1卷积后应用通道混洗。对于步长为2的单元，会使用额外的3×3平均池化进行下采样，并通过通道拼接（concatenation）而非相加（addition）来融合特征。

nodes.title: ShuffleNet整体架构
nodes.label: 网络架构
nodes.summary: 由多个阶段（Stage）组成的卷积神经网络，每个阶段包含多个ShuffleNet单元。
nodes.description: 网络从一个3×3卷积层和最大池化层开始，随后是三个主要阶段（Stage 2, 3, 4），每个阶段由多个ShuffleNet单元堆叠而成。每个阶段的第一个单元步长为2，用于下采样。通过调整每个阶段的输出通道数和分组数g，可以控制网络的复杂度和精度。瓶颈通道数（bottleneck channels）通常设置为输出通道数的1/4。

nodes.title: 复杂度缩放 (Complexity Scaling)
nodes.label: 设计策略
nodes.summary: 通过缩放因子s调整网络宽度，以适配不同的计算预算。
nodes.description: 为了将网络定制到所需的复杂度，可以简单地对通道数应用一个缩放因子s。例如，“ShuffleNet 1×”是基准网络，“ShuffleNet 0.5×”表示将所有通道数乘以0.5，从而将整体复杂度降低到约1/4。

edges.description: 逐点分组卷积是ShuffleNet单元的核心组成部分。
通道混洗操作被插入在ShuffleNet单元的两个逐点分组卷积之间。
多个ShuffleNet单元堆叠构成ShuffleNet整体架构的各个阶段。
复杂度缩放策略应用于ShuffleNet整体架构，以生成不同计算预算下的模型变体。

deltas.before: 在ResNeXt等架构中，1×1卷积是密集的（即标准卷积），计算成本高昂，占据了绝大部分计算量（如93.4%）。
deltas.after: 在ShuffleNet中，将1×1卷积替换为逐点分组卷积，大幅降低了其计算成本。
deltas.why_it_matters: 在极小网络（<150 MFLOPs）中，密集的1×1卷积严重限制了可使用的通道数，从而损害了模型容量和精度。逐点分组卷积使得在相同计算预算下可以使用更宽的特征图（更多通道），这对小网络至关重要。

deltas.before: 当多个分组卷积层堆叠时，输出通道仅与同一组内的输入通道相关，导致信息流在组间被阻塞，削弱了模型的表示能力。
deltas.after: 在分组卷积层之间引入通道混洗操作，对通道顺序进行重新排列，使得下一层的输入来自上一层的不同组。
deltas.why_it_matters: 通道混洗实现了跨组的信息流动，恢复了模型的表示能力，同时保持了分组卷积带来的计算效率。实验证明，该操作能显著提升分类精度，尤其在分组数较大时。

deltas.before: ResNet等架构的瓶颈单元使用密集的1×1卷积进行降维和升维。
deltas.after: ShuffleNet单元使用逐点分组卷积进行降维和升维，并在第一个1×1卷积后应用通道混洗。
deltas.why_it_matters: 这种设计使得ShuffleNet单元在相同设置下比ResNet和ResNeXt单元具有更低的计算复杂度（FLOPs），从而能在给定计算预算下构建更深或更宽的网络。

formulas.intuition: 计算一个标准ResNet瓶颈单元所需的浮点运算次数（乘加）。其中2cm项对应两个1×1卷积，9m²项对应一个3×3卷积。
计算一个ResNeXt瓶颈单元（使用分组卷积）所需的浮点运算次数。3×3卷积部分因分组而降低了计算量。
计算一个ShuffleNet单元所需的浮点运算次数。与ResNet/ResNeXt相比，其1×1卷积部分（2cm/g）和3×3卷积部分（9m）都因分组卷积和深度可分离卷积而大幅降低。这使得ShuffleNet在相同设置下复杂度最低。

glossary.逐点卷积 (Pointwise Convolution): 指1×1卷积，用于改变通道维度。
glossary.分组卷积 (Group Convolution): 将输入通道和输出通道分成若干组，每组独立进行卷积运算，以降低计算量。
glossary.通道混洗 (Channel Shuffle): 在分组卷积层之间对通道顺序进行重新排列的操作，以实现跨组信息流动。
glossary.深度可分离卷积 (Depthwise Separable Convolution: 一种高效卷积，包括逐通道卷积（Depthwise Convolution）和逐点卷积（Pointwise Convolution）。
glossary.瓶颈单元 (Bottleneck Unit): 一种网络结构，通过先降维再升维来减少计算量，如ResNet中的设计。
glossary.FLOPs: 浮点运算次数（Floating Point Operations），用于衡量模型计算复杂度。
glossary.缩放因子 (Scale Factor): 用于调整网络通道数以控制模型复杂度和精度的系数。
glossary.分组数 (Group Number, g): 在分组卷积中，将通道分成的组数。

metadata.abstract: We introduce an extremely computation-efficient CNN architecture named ShuffleNet, which is designed specially for mobile devices with very limited computing power (e.g., 10-150 MFLOPs). The new architecture utilizes two new operations, pointwise group convolution and channel shuffle, to greatly reduce computation cost while maintaining accuracy. Experiments on ImageNet classification and MS COCO object detection demonstrate the superior performance of ShuffleNet over other structures, e.g. lower top-1 error (absolute 7.8%) than recent MobileNet [12] on ImageNet classification task, under the computation budget of 40 MFLOPs. On an ARM-based mobile device, ShuffleNet achieves ~13Ã— actual speedup over AlexNet while maintaining comparable accuracy.

Abstract

We introduce an extremely computation-efﬁcient CNN architecture named ShufﬂeNet, which is designed specially for mobile devices with very limited computing power (e.g., 10-150 MFLOPs). We use exactly the same settings for all models to ensure fair comparisons. 4.1. Ablation Study The core idea of ShufﬂeNet lies in pointwise group con- volution and channel shufﬂe operation. In this subsection we evaluate them respectively.
4.1.1 Pointwise Group Convolutions

To evaluate the importance of pointwise group convolu- tions, we compare ShufﬂeNet models of the same com- plexity whose numbers of groups range from 1 to 8. If the group number equals 1, no pointwise group convolu- tion is involved and then the ShufﬂeNet unit becomes an ”Xception-like” [3] structure. For better understanding, we also scale the width of the networks to 3 different complex- ities and compare their classiﬁcation performance respec- tively. Results are shown in Table 2. From the results, we see that models with group convo- lutions (g > 1) consistently perform better than the coun-
terparts without pointwise group convolutions ( g = 1 ).
Smaller models tend to beneﬁt more from groups. For ex-
ample, for ShufﬂeNet 1 × the best entry ( g = 8 ) is 1.2%

better than the counterpart, while for ShufﬂeNet 0.5 × and 0.25× the gaps become 3.5% and 4.4% respectively. Note that group convolution allows more feature map channels for a given complexity constraint, so we hypothesize that the performance gain comes from wider feature maps which help to encode more information. In addition, a smaller network involves thinner feature maps, meaning it beneﬁts
more from enlarged feature maps.
Table 2 also shows that for some models (e.g. Shuf-
ﬂeNet 0.5 ×) when group numbers become relatively large
(e.g. g = 8 ), the classiﬁcation score saturates or even

drops. With an increase in group number (thus wider fea- ture maps), input channels for each convolutional ﬁlter be- come fewer, which may harm representation capability. In- terestingly, we also notice that for smaller models such as
ShufﬂeNet 0.25 × larger group numbers tend to better re-

sults consistently, which suggests wider feature maps bring more beneﬁts for smaller models. 4.1.2 Channel Shufﬂe vs. No Shufﬂe The purpose of shufﬂe operation is to enable cross-group information ﬂow for multiple group convolution layers. Ta- ble 3 compares the performance of ShufﬂeNet structures (group number is set to 3 or 8 for instance) with/without channel shufﬂe. The evaluations are performed under three different scales of complexity. It is clear that channel shuf- ﬂe consistently boosts classiﬁcation scores for different set-
tings. Especially, when group number is relatively large
(e.g. g = 8 ), models with channel shufﬂe outperform the
counterparts by a signiﬁcant margin, which shows the im-
portance of cross-group information interchange. 4.2. Comparison with Other Structure Units Recent leading convolutional units in VGG [30], ResNet [9], GoogleNet [33], ResNeXt [40] and Xcep-
tion [3] have pursued state-of-the-art results with large mod-
els (e.g. ≥ 1GFLOPs), but do not fully explore low-

Generalization Ability To evaluate the generalization ability for transfer learn- ing, we test our ShufﬂeNet model on the task of MS COCO object detection [23]. We adopt Faster-RCNN [28] as the detection framework and use the publicly released Caffe code [28, 17] for training with default settings. Similar to [12], the models are trained on the COCO train+val dataset
excluding 5000 minival images and we conduct testing on
the minival set. Table 7 shows the comparison of results
trained and evaluated on two input resolutions. Comparing ShufﬂeNet 2 × with MobileNet whose complexity are com-
parable (524 vs. 569 MFLOPs), our ShufﬂeNet 2 × sur-
passes MobileNet by a signiﬁcant margin on both resolu-

tions; our ShufﬂeNet 1 × also achieves comparable results with MobileNet on 600 × resolution, but has ∼4× com- plexity reduction. We conjecture that this signiﬁcant gain is partly due to ShufﬂeNet’s simple design of architecture without bells and whistles. 4.5. Actual Speedup Evaluation Finally, we evaluate the actual inference speed of Shuf- ﬂeNet models on a mobile device with an ARM platform.
Though ShufﬂeNets with larger group numbers (e.g. g = 4
or g = 8) usually have better performance, we ﬁnd it less
efﬁcient in our current implementation. Empirically g = 3

usually has a proper trade-off between accuracy and actual inference time. As shown in Table 8, three input resolutions are exploited for the test. Due to memory access and other overheads, we ﬁnd every 4× theoretical complexity reduc- tion usually results in ∼2.6× actual speedup in our im- plementation. Nevertheless, compared with AlexNet [21] our ShufﬂeNet 0.5 × model still achieves ∼13× actual speedup under comparable classiﬁcation accuracy (the the- oretical speedup is 18 ×), which is much faster than previ- ous AlexNet-level models or speedup approaches such as [14, 16, 22, 42, 43, 38].
